topics.title: sampling theorem
topics.essence: Sampling every T seconds copies the spectrum at every multiple of the sampling frequency. If the copies do not overlap, the original is still there, so sample faster than twice the highest frequency.
topics.check: A signal has nothing above 3 kHz. What is the slowest sampling rate that loses nothing, and what goes wrong just below it?

later.how: Data converters and multirate systems are designed by moving and filtering the spectral copies.

topics.title: aliasing
topics.essence: When the copies overlap, a frequency above half the sampling rate lands on top of a lower one and cannot be told apart from it afterwards.
topics.check: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. What frequency does it appear as?

later.how: Anti-aliasing filters and oversampling exist to control it.

topics.title: reconstruction
topics.essence: To get the signal back, keep one copy of the spectrum with a low-pass filter. In time, that is placing a sinc on every sample and adding them up.
topics.check: Between two samples, what decides the value of the rebuilt signal: its two neighbours only, or all the samples?

topics.title: zero-order hold
topics.essence: A practical converter holds each sample until the next one, making a staircase. Holding is itself a filter: it droops the top of the band and leaves faint images above it.
topics.check: What does the staircase contain that the smooth original does not, and where is it in frequency?

topics.title: digital filtering of analog signals
topics.essence: Sample, filter the numbers, then reconstruct. Below half the sampling rate the whole chain acts as one continuous-time filter: the digital filter's response with its frequency axis stretched by the sampling rate.
topics.check: A digital low-pass has its cutoff at π/4 rad per sample, and the sampling rate is 8 kHz. What is the cutoff of the whole chain in hertz?

topics.title: downsampling
topics.essence: Keep every Mth sample and the spectrum stretches by M. Anything above π/M beforehand folds back on top of the rest, so filter first.
topics.check: A sequence with content up to π/2 is downsampled by 3 with no filter. Does it alias? Why?

later.how: Decimators, interpolators and filter banks are built from these two operations.

topics.title: upsampling
topics.essence: Insert M − 1 zeros between samples and the spectrum squeezes by M, which brings M − 1 unwanted images into view. A low-pass filter removes them, and in time it fills in the zeros.
topics.check: One zero is inserted between each pair of samples. Where does the unwanted image sit before filtering?

links.why: Sampling is multiplying by an impulse train, which convolves the spectrum with another impulse train.
Multiplying in time by the sampling train is convolving in frequency, which makes the copies.
Aliasing is what the overlapping copies do.
Seen from the samples, a frequency and its alias are the same sequence.
If the copies do not overlap, a low-pass filter can keep one of them.
The filter that keeps exactly one copy is the ideal low-pass.
That filter's impulse response is the sinc placed on each sample.
Holding each sample is the crude interpolation that real converters use in place of the sinc.
With no aliasing, the samples carry the whole signal, so filtering the samples filters the signal.
The digital filter's response becomes the response of the whole chain.
Keeping every Mth sample is sampling again, and it aliases for the same reason.
The effect is read off the DTFT: stretched by M and added to its shifted copies.
Inserting zeros squeezes the DTFT by M.
The low-pass filter after the zeros is interpolation, the discrete version of reconstruction.
